# Let's test with REG_NEWLINE flag and more complex patterns
import ctypes
import ctypes.util

libc_path = ctypes.util.find_library('c')
libc = ctypes.CDLL(libc_path)

class regex_t(ctypes.Structure):
    _fields_ = [
        ('__buffer', ctypes.c_void_p),
        ('__allocated', ctypes.c_size_t),
        ('__used', ctypes.c_size_t),
        ('__syntax', ctypes.c_ulong),
        ('__fastmap', ctypes.c_char_p),
        ('__translate', ctypes.c_char_p),
        ('__re_nsub', ctypes.c_size_t),
        ('__bitfield', ctypes.c_char * 8),
    ]

class regmatch_t(ctypes.Structure):
    _fields_ = [
        ('rm_so', ctypes.c_int),
        ('rm_eo', ctypes.c_int),
    ]

libc.regcomp.argtypes = [ctypes.POINTER(regex_t), ctypes.c_char_p, ctypes.c_int]
libc.regcomp.restype = ctypes.c_int
libc.regexec.argtypes = [ctypes.POINTER(regex_t), ctypes.c_char_p, ctypes.c_size_t, ctypes.POINTER(regmatch_t), ctypes.c_int]
libc.regexec.restype = ctypes.c_int
libc.regfree.argtypes = [ctypes.POINTER(regex_t)]
libc.regfree.restype = None

REG_EXTENDED = 1
REG_NEWLINE = 2
REG_ICASE = 4

# Test patterns from the magic database with REG_EXTENDED|REG_NEWLINE
patterns = [
    (b'^[^Cc\ \t].*\$', 'fortran !'),
    (b'^[Cc][\ \t]', 'fortran C'),
    (b'^PROC', 'algol68 PROC'),
    (b'MODE[\t\ ]', 'algol68 MODE'),
    (b'REF[\t\ ]', 'algol68 REF'),
    (b'FLEX[\t\ ]\*\\\\[', 'algol68 FLEX'),
    (b'^import.*;\$', 'java import'),
    (b'^template[\ \t]+<.*>[\ \t\n]+', 'c-lang template'),
    (b'^[0-9]{1,50}\ [0-9]{1,50}', 'images netpbm'),
    (b'^[0-9]{1,50}', 'images size'),
    (b'^[0-9]*\ ', 'images zero-or-more'),
    (b'^[!-?A-~]{1,255}(\t[^\t]+){11}', 'bioinformatics SAM'),
    (b'^([^\t]+\t){1}[0-9]{1,5}\t', 'bioinformatics'),
    (b'^([^\t]+\t){2}\\\\*|[^*=]*\t', 'bioinformatics CIGAR'),
    (b'^[@]HD\t.*VN:', 'bioinformatics HD'),
    (b'^[\ \t]*require[\ \t][A-Za-z_/]+', 'ruby require'),
    (b'^[\ \t]*(class|module)[\ \t][A-Z]', 'ruby class'),
    (b'^#!.*/bin/perl([[:space:]].*)*\$', 'perl'),
    (b'^from[\040\t\f\r\n]+([A-Za-z0-9_]|\\\\.)+[\040\t\f\r\n]+import.*\$', 'python'),
    (b'^[0-9]', 'psdbms'),
    (b'^[\ \t]{0,10}call[\ \t]{1,10}rxfunc', 'msdos rexx call'),
    (b'^[\ \t]{0,10}say\ [\"\\']', 'msdos rexx say'),
]

for pattern, name in patterns:
    regex = regex_t()
    rc = libc.regcomp(ctypes.byref(regex), pattern, REG_EXTENDED | REG_NEWLINE)
    if rc != 0:
        print(f'{name}: regcomp failed with {rc}')
        continue
    
    # Test with empty string
    pmatch = regmatch_t()
    pmatch.rm_so = -1
    pmatch.rm_eo = -1
    rc = libc.regexec(ctypes.byref(regex), b'', 1, ctypes.byref(pmatch), 0)
    print(f'{name}: regexec rc={rc}, pmatch=({pmatch.rm_so}, {pmatch.rm_eo})')
    
    libc.regfree(ctypes.byref(regex))
"` executed with exit code 0.

message.content:
Interesting! On this glibc version, all patterns that match empty string DO initialize pmatch. So the bug might be specific to certain glibc versions or certain patterns.

Let me look at this from a different angle. The bug description says "A bug in glibc/regex/msan causes regexec to return 0 but not initialize pmatch." This is a known MSan finding. Let me look at the actual glibc bug report:
